title: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
summary: Move sensor readings from devices through MQTT and Kafka into windowed stream processing, handle out-of-order and late data with watermarks, filter and flag online, downsample, and get the guarantees right.
outcomes: Explain why sensor pipelines must window by event time and how a watermark decides when a window fires
Compute which readings are on time, late or dropped given an out-of-orderness bound and allowed lateness
Compute an EMA and Welford running mean and variance online, and explain the EMA as an IIR low-pass
Choose MQTT QoS, Kafka keys and partitions, and rollup and retention settings for a sensor fleet
Explain what end-to-end exactly-once requires and why at-least-once paths need idempotent writes

lessons.title: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order

blocks.md:
A sensor pipeline moves a continuous flow of readings (temperature, vibration, power) from devices to storage and analytics. The data never ends, so you cannot wait for "all of it" before computing. Worse, it does not arrive in the order it was measured: devices batch messages, radios drop and retry, gateways go offline and later flush a backlog, and every hop has queues.

This course builds such a pipeline step by step: ingest, buffering, windowed aggregation with watermarks, online filtering, anomaly flags, downsampling and delivery guarantees.

blocks.title: A typical sensor pipeline, edge to storage

scenes.caption: Sensors measure and publish small messages. Each reading carries the time the device measured it: its event time.
A lightweight MQTT broker accepts the device connections. A bridge copies messages into a Kafka topic, keyed by device id so one device's readings stay in one partition.
The stream processor reads the log, groups readings into event-time windows, filters them and flags anomalies. The time it sees each record is its processing time.
Results go to a time-series database (downsampled, with retention) and to an alerting path. Every hop adds delay, buffering and a chance of duplicates.

blocks.md:
Every reading has two timestamps. The Dataflow paper (Akidau et al., VLDB 2015) defines **event time** as "the time at which the event itself actually occurred", recorded by the clock of the system that generated it, and **processing time** as "the time at which an event is observed at any given point during processing", by the pipeline's clock.

Event time of a reading never changes. Processing time keeps growing as the record flows through each stage. The gap between the two is the **skew**, and it varies from record to record.

blocks.title: Twelve readings from one sensor, in arrival order

scenes.caption: The processor sees these 12 temperature readings in this order (arrival = processing time). The device stamped each with its own event time.
Delay is arrival minus event time. Most readings take under a second, but e3, e6, e8 and e10 take 3 to 6 s, and e12 arrives 21.6 s late (the sensor was offline and buffered it).
Out of order: e3 (t = 2) arrives after e2 (t = 4); e6 (t = 9) after e5 (t = 13); e8, e10 and e12 likewise. Sorting by arrival does not sort by event time.

blocks.md: Here is the toy stream the whole course uses: one temperature sensor, 12 readings. Suppose you want the mean temperature for each 10 second interval. The naive approach buckets readings by when they arrive, which is easy because arrivals are in order. The figure below shows why that answers the wrong question.

blocks.title: Mean temperature per 10 s window: two clocks, two answers

scenes.caption: Processing-time windows (bucket by arrival): 20.2, 22.375, 21.1. The 20-30 s bucket includes e10 (measured at 19 s) and e12 (measured at 7 s).
Event-time windows over all 12 readings (bucket by measurement time): 20.367, 22.45, 21.35. Same data, different answer; only these describe what the sensor saw in each interval.

blocks.md: Window by **event time** (when the device measured) whenever the result should describe the physical world. Processing time describes your pipeline, not your sensor: a network hiccup would change a temperature average.

Event time has its own catch: it is only as good as the device clock. Cheap devices drift, reboot to a default date, or never synced their clock. A clock running behind makes fresh readings look late; a clock running ahead stamps readings in the future. Common defenses are syncing device clocks (for example with NTP), having the gateway stamp an ingestion time as a fallback, and rejecting or clamping timestamps that are implausibly far from the ingestion time.

Misconception: "out of order is rare, so I can ignore it". In the toy, 5 of 12 readings arrive after a reading with a later event time. Mobile, battery-powered and intermittently connected devices make this the normal case, not an edge case.

blocks.question: A gateway loses its uplink for 30 s and then forwards all buffered readings at once. You compute per-10 s averages by processing time. What happens to the 30 s of readings?
options: They are averaged into the windows in which they were measured, just later
They all land in the single window in which they arrived, and the three earlier windows show missing data
Kafka reorders them by event time before the processor sees them
MQTT QoS 1 guarantees they are delivered in event-time order
blocks.explain: Processing-time windows bucket by arrival. The burst lands in one window (inflating its count) and the earlier windows look empty. Kafka keeps the order in which records were written to a partition; it does not sort by event time.

blocks.question: Which timestamp should you use to decide whether a machine overheated between 14:00:00 and 14:00:10?
options: Processing time at the stream processor
Kafka's append time for the record
The event time the sensor stamped on the reading
The time the database row was written
blocks.explain: Only the event time refers to when the physical measurement happened. The other three are processing times at different stages, each shifted by network and queueing delay.

lessons.title: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle

blocks.md:
Devices are small, battery powered and on flaky links, so they usually speak **MQTT**: a publish/subscribe protocol where clients publish messages to named topics on a broker, and subscribers receive messages for topics they subscribed to. The MQTT 5.0 spec says it runs "over TCP/IP, or over other network protocols that provide ordered, lossless, bi-directional connections".

Each message is published with a **Quality of Service** level:

- **QoS 0, at most once**: sent once, no acknowledgment. Can be lost.
- **QoS 1, at least once**: the receiver answers PUBACK; the sender keeps the message and, after a reconnect, re-sends it until PUBACK arrives. Never lost, but duplicates can occur.
- **QoS 2, exactly once**: a four-packet handshake (PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP) so the message arrives once.

blocks.title: MQTT QoS 1: a lost acknowledgment creates a duplicate

scenes.caption: QoS 1 (at least once): the sensor sends PUBLISH with a packet id and keeps the message until it gets PUBACK.
The broker forwards the message to its subscriber and acknowledges, but the PUBACK is lost (for example, the radio link drops).
The sensor reconnects, resuming its session, and re-sends the unacknowledged PUBLISH (MQTT 5 only resends on reconnect). The spec requires the DUP flag set to 1 on a re-delivery.
The broker cannot tell that it already forwarded this message, so the subscriber receives e7 twice. Nothing was lost, but downstream must tolerate duplicates.

blocks.md: QoS applies per hop: sensor to broker, and broker to each subscriber. The spec says a message delivered to a subscriber gets the minimum of the QoS it was published with and the maximum QoS granted to that subscription. So a QoS 2 publish to a QoS 0 subscription is delivered at QoS 0. QoS 2 costs two round trips per message, which is why many fleets use QoS 1 and make the downstream tolerate duplicates.

The broker is a router, not a durable history. The middle of the pipeline is usually a **Kafka** topic: an append-only log split into **partitions** spread across brokers. Kafka's docs state that events with the same key "are written to the same partition", and that a consumer reads a partition's events in exactly the order they were written. There is no order across partitions.

Consumed events are not deleted. Retention is a per-topic setting (by time or size), so a new job can replay last week's readings. A common production setting is replication factor 3, meaning three copies of each partition.

blocks.title: Kafka: keys pick partitions, a consumer group splits them

scenes.caption: Records with the same key always go to the same partition, so all of sensor A's readings are in partition 0, in the order they were written.
Within one consumer group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer. Here consumer 1 owns partitions 0 and 1, consumer 2 owns partition 2.
If consumer 2 fails, the group reassigns partition 2 to consumer 1, which resumes from the last committed offset. Records stay in the log, so nothing is lost; some may be read again.

blocks.md: Per-partition order is *write* order, not event-time order. If sensor A's readings were written late (e12 in our toy), they sit in the log after newer ones. Kafka removes the network chaos between bridge and processor, but it cannot undo disorder that happened before the write.

A consumer tracks its **offset** per partition: a single integer, the position of the next record to read. Because that state is tiny, it can be checkpointed cheaply, and rewinding it replays data.

What happens when a stage is slower than its input? In Flink, a task whose output buffers are full is **backpressured**: it stops sending, its input buffers fill, and the slowdown propagates upstream until the source reads more slowly. With Kafka in front, nothing is dropped: records simply wait in the log, and the waiting amount is the **consumer lag**.

scenes.caption: 5000 records/s arrive, 4000/s are processed. The gap of 1000/s piles up: after 10 minutes, 600,000 records wait in Kafka.
When processing keeps up (rate at least equal to arrivals), lag stays at zero. Backpressure only matters while the input rate exceeds what the slowest stage can absorb.
A 7000/s burst against 4000/s: lag grows 3000/s, 1.8 million records in 10 minutes. Once the burst ends, the backlog drains at (processing minus arrival) per second.

blocks.md:
A simple fluid model makes the arithmetic clear (simplified: real arrivals are bursty and processing rates vary). With arrival rate $\lambda$ and processing rate $\mu$, the lag after an overload of duration $t$ is $(\lambda - \mu)\,t$. With 5000 records/s in and 4000/s processed for 10 minutes, lag is 600,000 records. If input then drops to 3000/s, the backlog drains at 1000/s, taking another 600 s.

Two rules follow. Retention must exceed the worst lag you will ever accumulate, or unread data is deleted. And a lagging pipeline produces late results, which in event time looks like slow watermarks (next lesson).

Kafka turns backpressure from data loss into delay: as long as retention covers the backlog, a slow consumer only falls behind. The bounded buffers inside the processor are what make the slowdown propagate instead of growing memory without bound.

blocks.question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group with 6 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
options: 6: Kafka splits each partition across consumers
1: only the group leader reads
4: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so 2 sit idle
12: every consumer reads every partition
blocks.explain: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a group. With more consumers than partitions, the extras get nothing. Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.

blocks.question: Sensors publish at QoS 1. Your rollup job sums energy readings per minute and the totals are occasionally slightly too high. Most likely cause?
options: QoS 1 can lose messages, and losses push sums up
QoS 1 retries after a lost PUBACK, so a reading can be delivered twice and counted twice
Kafka reorders records within a partition
MQTT always runs over UDP, which duplicates packets
blocks.explain: At least once means no loss but possible duplicates. A sum counts a duplicate twice. The fix is to deduplicate on a reading id (device id plus sequence number) or to write results idempotently, covered in the last lesson.

lessons.title: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step

blocks.md: A **window** slices an endless stream into finite chunks you can aggregate. The Dataflow paper names three common shapes. **Fixed** windows (also called tumbling) have a static size, such as hourly. **Sliding** windows have a size and a slide period, such as hourly windows starting every minute, so they overlap. **Sessions** capture a period of activity per key and end after a gap of inactivity. In Flink, tumbling and sliding windows are aligned to the epoch unless you give an offset.

blocks.title: Three window shapes over the same 30 s of event time

scenes.caption: Tumbling (fixed) windows: fixed size, no overlap, aligned. Every reading belongs to exactly one window: [0,10), [10,20), [20,30).
Sliding windows: size 10 s, a new one every 5 s, so they overlap and each reading belongs to 2 windows (drawn on two lanes). Useful for a smooth "last 10 s" metric updated every 5 s.
Session windows: no fixed size; a session ends after a gap of inactivity. With a 4 s gap, our readings at 1, 2, 4, ... 22 s form one session and the reading at 27 s (5 s after 22) starts another.

blocks.md:
With event-time windows a new question appears: when is window [0,10) complete? Readings for it may still be in flight. Stream processors answer with a **watermark**: a moving marker in event time. In Flink's words, a watermark with timestamp $t$ declares that event time has reached $t$ in that stream, meaning no more elements with timestamp at or below $t$ are expected.

The Dataflow paper stresses that for most real sources the watermark is a *heuristic* guess, because the system cannot know when an offline device will reconnect.

The most common heuristic is **bounded out-of-orderness**: assume readings are at most $B$ late. Flink's `forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration)` strategy does this, and its documented example generator emits the maximum timestamp seen minus the bound minus 1 ms. We drop the 1 ms and use whole seconds:

blocks.tex: W = \max_{\text{seen}} t_{\text{event}} - B, \qquad \text{fire } [s, s+10) \text{ when } W \ge s + 10, \qquad \text{delete it when } W \ge s + 10 + L
blocks.caption: B is the out-of-orderness bound (2 s here). L is the allowed lateness (5 s here). Simplified: Flink emits watermarks periodically rather than after every record.

blocks.md: A reading is **late** if it arrives after the watermark has passed the end of its window. Flink's default allowed lateness is 0, so late elements are dropped. With allowed lateness $L > 0$, Flink keeps the window's state until the watermark passes end plus $L$; a late but not dropped element makes the window fire again with an updated result. Anything later than that is dropped, or routed to a **side output** if you ask for one.

blocks.prompt: e6 (t = 9) arrives at processing time 14.0 s, after e5 (t = 13) has pushed the watermark to 11. Window [0,10) has already fired with 4 readings. What happens to e6?
blocks.reveal: With allowed lateness 0, e6 would be dropped: the watermark (11) is past the window end (10). With allowed lateness 5, the window's state lives until W reaches 15, so e6 is added and the window **fires a second time** with count 5 and mean 20.32 instead of 20.2. Downstream receives two results for the same window and must treat the second as a correction.

blocks.title: Tumbling 10 s windows, B = 2 s, allowed lateness 5 s

scenes.caption: Rules for this walk-through: watermark W = (max event time seen) minus 2. A window [s, s+10) fires when W reaches s+10; its state is kept until W reaches s+15 (5 s allowed lateness), then deleted.
e1 to e4 arrive. e3 (t = 2) is out of order, but W is only 2 when it arrives, far below 10, so it simply joins window [0,10). After e4, max = 8 and W = 6.
e5 (t = 13) raises max to 13, so W = 11 and passes 10: window [0,10) fires with e1 to e4: count 4, mean 20.2 C.
e6 (t = 9) arrives with W = 11: behind the watermark, so late. But 11 < 10 + 5, so the window still exists. The reading is added and the window fires again: count 5, mean 20.32 C.
e7 (t = 16) moves W to 14. e8 (t = 11) is out of order but 14 < 20, so it is on time for window [10,20).
e9 (t = 22) moves W to 20. Window [10,20) fires with e5, e7, e8: mean 22.9, max 26.5. Window [0,10) passes 10 + 5 = 15, so its state is deleted.
e10 (t = 19) is late (W = 20 is past 20) but within lateness (20 < 25). Window [10,20) fires again: count 4, mean 22.45.
e11 (t = 27) moves W to 25, so window [10,20) is now deleted too. Then e12 (t = 7) arrives, 21.6 s after it was measured. Its window was deleted at W = 15: dropped (or sent to a side output).
Final tally: 9 on time, 2 late but accepted (e6, e10), 1 dropped (e12). Window [20,30) holds e9 and e11 and will fire only when W reaches 30.

blocks.md:
The repeated firings raise a design question the Dataflow paper calls **accumulation mode**: how does a later result for a window relate to an earlier one?

- **Discarding**: each firing emits only what arrived since the last one (e6 alone).
- **Accumulating**: each firing emits the full refined result (count 5, mean 20.32); the consumer overwrites the old value.
- **Accumulating and retracting**: emit a retraction of the old value, then the new one, so a downstream aggregation can subtract it.

The paper also generalizes "fire when the watermark passes" into **triggers**: rules for when in processing time to emit, such as early results every minute plus a final one at the watermark.

Two different knobs, often confused. The bound $B$ moves the watermark (how long to wait before the first result). The allowed lateness $L$ keeps state after that (how long to accept corrections). Raising $B$ delays every result; raising $L$ costs state memory and extra firings but does not delay the first result.

The Dataflow paper notes watermarks fail in two directions. **Too fast**: late data arrives behind it (e12). **Too slow**: a single slow input holds back progress for everything. In Flink, an operator with several inputs takes the **minimum** of their watermarks, and with Kafka the watermark is tracked per partition. A partition that receives no data never advances, freezing every window downstream, which is what `withIdleness` addresses by marking such inputs idle.

blocks.prompt: A sensor with a misconfigured clock sends one reading stamped 60 s in the future, between e7 and e8. With B = 2 s, what happens?
blocks.reveal: The maximum event time jumps to 76 (16 + 60), so W jumps to 74. Window [10,20) fires at once with only e5 and e7, and because W is already past end plus 5, its state and that of [0,10) (which already fired) are deleted immediately. Then e8 (t = 11), e9, e10, e11 and e12 all arrive behind a watermark that is far past their windows' cleanup point: **all dropped**. One bad clock silently discards correct data from every other reading that shares that watermark. Clamp or reject timestamps far ahead of ingestion time before they reach the watermark generator.

blocks.md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

blocks.question: Rerun the toy with B = 7 s instead of 2 s (L still 5 s). Which readings are late or dropped?
options: e6 and e10 late, e12 dropped, exactly as before
No reading is late, and e12 is still dropped
Nothing is late or dropped
Every out-of-order reading is dropped
blocks.explain: When e6 arrives, max = 13 so W = 6 < 10: on time. When e10 arrives, max = 22 so W = 15 < 20: on time. e12 arrives with W = 27 - 7 = 20, past 10 + 5 = 15: still dropped. The price: window [0,10) now first fires at processing time 22.5 s (when e9 arrives) instead of 13.4 s.

blocks.question: A Flink job reads a Kafka topic with 8 partitions. One partition stops receiving data. Per-minute windows stop producing results for all sensors. Why?
options: Kafka blocks all partitions when one is empty
Allowed lateness is too large
Tumbling windows require data in every partition
The operator's watermark is the minimum over its inputs, and the idle partition's watermark never advances
blocks.explain: Watermarks are tracked per partition and combined with a minimum. A silent partition pins the minimum, so no window end is ever passed. Marking idle inputs (withIdleness) lets the watermark advance without them.

lessons.title: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags

blocks.md: Windows give you summaries every few seconds. Many sensor jobs also need per-reading answers: a smoothed value for a dashboard, a flag when a reading is abnormal. In a stream these must be **online**: one pass, constant memory per sensor, an update per reading. You cannot store the history and recompute.

The workhorse smoother is the **exponentially weighted moving average** (EMA, called EWMA in the NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook). With smoothing constant $\alpha$ ($0 < \alpha \le 1$), each new reading $x_n$ updates the output:

blocks.caption: Unrolling the recursion shows the weights decay geometrically: with alpha = 0.3 they are 0.3, 0.21, 0.147, 0.103, ... The NIST handbook notes alpha between 0.2 and 0.3 as a common choice for EWMA charts.

blocks.md: From the signal processing prereq: an EMA is a first-order **IIR** (infinite impulse response) filter, because the output feeds back into itself. Its transfer function and frequency response are

blocks.caption: f is in cycles per sample. At f = 0 the gain is 1; at the Nyquist frequency 0.5 it is alpha / (2 - alpha). So the EMA is a low-pass filter.

blocks.title: EMA frequency response: a first-order low-pass

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.3: gain 1 at f = 0 (a constant passes unchanged), falling to 0.707 near 0.057 cycles per sample and to 0.176 at the Nyquist frequency 0.5.
alpha = 0.1: heavier smoothing. The -3 dB point drops to about 0.017 cycles per sample, so only very slow changes pass; the cost is lag.
alpha = 0.5: lighter smoothing, -3 dB near 0.115 cycles per sample. With alpha = 1 the gain is 1 everywhere: no filtering at all.

blocks.title: EMA with alpha = 0.3, updated as each reading arrives

scenes.caption: Initialize with the first reading: y = 20.0. Each update is y = 0.3 x + 0.7 y. The only state is one number.
e2 to e4: y moves 30 percent of the way toward each reading: 20.03, 20.111, 20.198.
e5 is a spike of 26.5. The EMA rises only to 22.088: 0.3 x 26.5 + 0.7 x 20.198. A low-pass filter attenuates a one-sample jump.
After the spike, the EMA decays back toward about 21.3; each step keeps 70 percent of the previous excess. Final value 21.092.

blocks.prompt: The EMA above ran in arrival order and ended at 21.092. Run the same 12 readings in event-time order instead. Same final value?
blocks.reveal: No: 21.54 instead of 21.092. The EMA weights recent inputs most, so its output depends on order. In arrival order the last input is e12 (20.6, measured at 7 s); in event order the last is e11 (21.3, measured at 27 s). For a smoother that should reflect the physical signal, feed it event-ordered data (for example per window after the watermark passes), or accept that late readings are applied out of sequence.

blocks.md: Real sensors are not sampled at perfectly even intervals, so a fixed $\alpha$ weights a 3 s gap the same as a 1 s gap. A common fix comes from the continuous first-order low-pass with time constant $\tau$: holding the input constant over a gap of $\Delta t$ and solving exactly gives $\alpha = 1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau}$. With $\tau = 3$ s, a 1 s gap gives $\alpha = 0.2835$ and a 3 s gap gives $0.6321$.

For anomaly flags you need the running mean and variance. The textbook one-pass formula, sum of squares minus $n$ times the squared mean, subtracts two large nearly equal numbers. Chan, Golub and LeVeque (Stanford, 1979) point out that this can cause gross cancellation and even negative variances, whereas **updating** formulas add a nonnegative term at each step. Welford's update (1962) is the standard one:

blocks.caption: Three numbers of state per sensor (n, mean, M2). The added term delta times (x minus new mean) is never negative.

blocks.title: Welford's update over the first readings
blocks.code:
def welford_update(state, x):
    n, mean, m2 = state
    n += 1
    delta = x - mean          # distance to old mean
    mean += delta / n
    delta2 = x - mean         # distance to new mean
    m2 += delta * delta2      # sum of squared deviations
    return (n, mean, m2)

def variance(state):
    n, mean, m2 = state
    return m2 / (n - 1)       # sample variance

def is_anomaly(state, x, k=3.0, warmup=4):
    n, mean, m2 = state
    if n < warmup:
        return False
    z = (x - mean) / variance(state) ** 0.5
    return abs(z) > k

scenes.caption: State starts at n = 0, mean = 0, m2 = 0. Reading e1 = 20.0 arrives.
First reading: delta = 20.0, mean becomes 20.0, delta2 = 0, so m2 stays 0. One point has no spread.
e4 = 20.4: delta = 0.2667, mean = 20.2, delta2 = 0.2, m2 = 0.1. Sample variance = 0.1 / 3 = 0.0333, standard deviation 0.1826.
e5 = 26.5 arrives. Before updating, check it against the current stats: n = 4 meets the warm-up, z = (26.5 - 20.2) / 0.1826 = 34.5. Flagged as an anomaly.
Then update with e5: delta = 6.3, mean = 21.46, delta2 = 5.04, m2 = 0.1 + 31.752 = 31.852. Variance jumps to 7.963 (sd 2.822).
After all 12 readings: n = 12, mean = 21.225, m2 = 32.8025, variance 2.982. A two-pass computation gives the same values, in any arrival order.

blocks.md: The flag in the code is a **z-score** test: compare each reading to the statistics of the readings *before* it, $z = (x - \bar{x})/s$, and flag when $|z| > 3$ after a warm-up. The order of check-then-update matters: updating first would let the reading vote on whether it is normal.

blocks.title: Running standard deviation after each reading

scenes.caption: Before the spike the sensor's spread is 0.18 C. One 26.5 reading lifts it to 2.82 C, and it decays only slowly as normal readings accumulate.
Masking: after e12 the sd is still 1.73 C, so a new reading of 25.0 C (almost 4 C above normal) scores z = 2.19 and is not flagged. The spike made the detector blind.

blocks.md: Two opposite failure modes. **Masking**: if flagged readings update the stats, one spike inflates the variance and hides later anomalies (above). **Lockout**: if flagged readings are skipped, a genuine level shift is flagged forever; in our data, skipping flagged readings makes e6 to e11 (all near 21 C) score z between 3.3 and 6.6 against a 4-reading warm-up. Real detectors use longer warm-ups, decaying statistics, or robust measures.
Online operators keep O(1) state per key and update per reading. Mean and variance via Welford are order-independent; the EMA is not. Both are cheap enough to run per sensor in the stream processor.

blocks.question: You set alpha = 0.05 on a vibration sensor sampled at 100 Hz to remove noise. Operators complain the smoothed signal reacts to real changes too slowly. What is the tradeoff?
options: Small alpha lowers the cutoff frequency: more noise removed, but more lag
Small alpha raises the cutoff frequency, so it should react faster; the bug is elsewhere
Alpha only affects the DC gain, not the response time
An EMA has no lag because it is computed online
blocks.explain: The EMA's gain falls off above a cutoff that shrinks with alpha. Heavy smoothing means the output needs many samples to follow a step: weights decay as (1 - alpha) to the k, so with alpha = 0.05 a step is still about 36 percent unfollowed after 20 samples.

blocks.question: Two parallel tasks each computed Welford state for half of a sensor's readings. Can you get the exact overall variance?
options: No, variance needs all raw values in one place
Yes, by averaging the two variances
Yes, by combining (n, mean, M2) of both halves with a pairwise merge formula
Only if both halves have the same mean
blocks.explain: Averaging variances ignores the difference between the two means. Chan, Golub and LeVeque give a merge: M2 = M2a + M2b + delta squared x na x nb / (na + nb), with delta the difference of means. This is what makes mean and variance easy to parallelize across partitions.

lessons.title: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once

blocks.md: Raw sensor data is large and its value decays: you need every reading from the last hour to debug a device, but only per-minute summaries from last year. Time-series databases build this in. InfluxDB's guide pairs **retention policies** (delete data older than a duration) with **continuous queries** that periodically aggregate and write results elsewhere. Its example keeps 10 second data for two hours and 30 minute means for 52 weeks.

TimescaleDB's **continuous aggregates** are materialized aggregates, typically grouped with `time_bucket`, that are refreshed automatically in the background and incrementally: changes to older data invalidate only the affected buckets, which are then recomputed. They can be stacked (minute rollups feeding hourly ones). Unlike a stream window, a database bucket has no watermark, so a late reading like e12 still updates its bucket at the next refresh, as long as that bucket lies inside the refresh policy's window (start_offset).

blocks.title: Downsampling 12 raw rows into 10 s rollups

scenes.caption: The database stores all 12 readings by event time, including e12 (20.6): an insert has no watermark, so late data still lands in its bucket. Buckets 0-10 s, 10-20 s, 20-30 s hold 6, 4 and 2 readings.
A rollup keeps a few numbers per bucket: count 6, 4, 2; mean 20.367, 22.45, 21.35. The 0-10 s mean differs from the stream job's 20.32 because the stream dropped e12.
Keep min and max too. The 10-20 s mean of 22.45 hides that one reading hit 26.5; the max preserves the spike after the raw rows are gone.

Retention then deletes the raw rows after a short period while rollups are kept much longer. 12 rows became 3; at one reading per second per sensor, a 10 s rollup has 10x fewer rows, a 1 minute rollup 60x fewer.

blocks.md: Store mergeable parts (count, sum, min, max, and M2 if you need variance), not just the mean. The mean of the first two rollups above is (20.367 + 22.45) / 2 = 21.408, but the true mean of those 10 readings is (6 x 20.367 + 4 x 22.45) / 10 = 21.2. Weighting by count needs the count.

Now the guarantee question. Kafka's design docs define three delivery semantics:

- **At most once**: messages may be lost but are never redelivered (commit the position, then process).
- **At least once**: never lost, possibly redelivered (process, then commit). This is Kafka's default.
- **Exactly once**: each message's effect happens once. Kafka achieves it with an idempotent producer (the broker deduplicates retries using a producer id and sequence numbers) and transactions that write output and consumer offsets atomically, read by consumers with `isolation.level=read_committed`.

Flink's exactly-once is about its **state**. It periodically draws consistent snapshots by injecting barriers at the sources (a scheme based on Chandy-Lamport). On failure it restores the latest checkpoint and rewinds the sources, for example to stored Kafka offsets, and replays. Internal state then reflects each record once. Effects *outside* Flink, like rows in a database, are a different matter.

blocks.title: Crash and replay: at-least-once vs exactly-once output

scenes.caption: The job reads sensor records from offset 40 and checkpoints its state together with the source offset.
It reads 50-59, fires window [10,20) and writes count 4, mean 22.45 to the sink. Then it crashes before the next checkpoint completes.
Recovery restores the last checkpoint (offset 50) and rewinds the source. Records 50-59 are processed again and the window fires again.

With a plain append (INSERT) the sink now has two rows for the same window: at-least-once. An upsert keyed by (sensor, window) or a transactional sink that commits only with the checkpoint makes the effect happen once.

blocks.prompt: MQTT QoS 1 delivered e7 (21.2 C) twice into window [10,20), and the job does not deduplicate. Using the final accepted set e5, e7, e8, e10, what mean does the window report?
blocks.reveal: Count 5 instead of 4, mean (26.5 + 21.2 + 21.2 + 21.0 + 21.1) / 5 = **22.2** instead of 22.45. Checkpoints cannot fix this: the duplicate entered *before* the pipeline's exactly-once boundary, so to the job it is a distinct record. Only deduplication on a reading id (device id plus a per-device sequence number) removes it.

blocks.md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

Misconception: "QoS 2 at the device makes the pipeline exactly-once". MQTT QoS covers one hop. The bridge, Kafka producer, stream job and sink each need their own guarantee, and a single at-least-once hop reintroduces duplicates.

blocks.question: Your sink appends one row per window firing. With allowed lateness 5 s, window [0,10) fires at count 4 and later at count 5. A dashboard sums all rows per window. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
options: The window is counted as 4 + 5 = 9 readings; write with an upsert keyed by (sensor, window) since firings are accumulating
Nothing; the second firing contains only the late reading
Late firings are never sent to sinks
The fix is to set allowed lateness higher
blocks.explain: In accumulating mode each firing is the full refined result, so appending both rows double counts. Overwrite by window key, or use discarding mode and have the consumer add deltas, or emit retractions.

blocks.question: Which design gives the most useful long-term history for detecting rare overheating at the lowest storage cost?
options: Keep raw readings forever
Keep raw data for days and 1-minute rollups with count, mean, min and max for years
Keep only 1-hour means for years
Keep only the latest reading per sensor
blocks.explain: Short raw retention covers debugging, and long-lived rollups with min and max keep the extremes that a mean hides, at a fraction of the rows. Hourly means alone would average away a 30 second overheat.

blocks.question: A consumer commits its Kafka offset immediately after reading a batch and before writing results. It crashes mid-write. What semantics did you get?
options: Exactly once
At least once
At most once: the batch's unwritten results are lost
No effect, Kafka rolls back the commit
blocks.explain: Committing before processing means on restart the consumer resumes after the batch; anything not yet written is never processed. Kafka's docs describe this as the at-most-once pattern.
